note.text: Hot deserts have severe water limitation, often with low and unreliable rainfall and high evaporative demand. Many lie in subtropical belts, such as the Sahara, but position, rain shadows and ocean influences matter. Ground may be rocky, stony or sandy; deserts are not all sand dunes. Vegetation is usually sparse, with adaptations such as reduced leaves, water storage, deep or spreading roots and rapid growth after rain. Some animals avoid daytime heat or conserve water. Not every desert is hot, though this lesson concerns hot deserts.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text: By the end, you should be able to explain aridity and adaptations and distinguish low rainfall from absence of life. Builds on: seasonal moisture limitation and monsoon contrasts. Leads to: Mediterranean drought and the drier parts of Cameroon.

sections.heading: Follow the local example or model
sections.text: An invented desert chart has very small monthly amounts. Its annual total illustrates dryness, while temperature and evaporation evidence would strengthen a water-deficit explanation. Oases concentrate water locally; they do not remove aridity across the whole desert. Pastoralism and irrigated cultivation face water and land constraints. Overuse of scarce water or poor drainage under irrigation can create additional problems, including salinity.

sections.heading: Apply and check
sections.text: Explain each adaptation’s relationship to water or heat without claiming that all plants share it. Distinguish drought, a temporary shortage relative to usual conditions, from aridity, a long-term climatic condition. The Far North of Cameroon includes semi-arid landscapes; do not label the entire region a true hot desert merely because it has a long dry season.

key_words.meaning: a long-term climatic shortage of available moisture
a feature reducing loss or improving access to scarce water
a concentration of accessible water within a drier landscape
rocky stony and sandy surfaces rather than dunes alone

mistake.wrong: One rain shower permanently ends climatic aridity.
mistake.right: a long-term climatic shortage of available moisture.
mistake.why: A brief event does not replace the longer-term moisture regime.

cards.idea: Distinguish the features before applying them.
example: aridity: a long-term climatic shortage of available moisture.
water-conserving adaptation: a feature reducing loss or improving access to scarce water.
local water source: a concentration of accessible water within a drier landscape.
surface diversity: rocky stony and sandy surfaces rather than dunes alone.

cards.idea: Use the evidence in the example, not a place name alone.
example: A desert region receives little reliable rain relative to evaporative demand.
A model plant has reduced leaves and a water-storing stem.
An oasis supports growth around a water supply.
A desert photograph shows bare rock and gravel instead of sand dunes.

cards.idea: Explain how the process produces the stated effect.
example: A brief event does not replace the longer-term moisture regime.
Adaptations differ but commonly address scarce moisture or high heat loads.
A local supply can support life without changing regional aridity.
Desert classification concerns aridity, not one required surface material.

questions.prompt: Read the invented monthly rainfall chart. Add the labels above all monthly bars to obtain the annual total in mm; the vertical-axis tick labels are not extra observations.

misconceptions.explain: That is a monthly mean, not the sum for the year.
That is the difference between wettest and driest months, not the annual total.
That multiplies an already millimetre total by ten without a unit conversion.

solution: The annual rainfall of this classroom record is {answer} mm. A real biome classification also needs temperature and other evidence.

right.text: aridity: a long-term climatic shortage of available moisture.
right.explain: This distinction is correct: A brief event does not replace the longer-term moisture regime. Look for a claim that reverses the process or makes an unsupported generalisation.

right.text: water-conserving adaptation: a feature reducing loss or improving access to scarce water.
right.explain: This distinction is correct: Adaptations differ but commonly address scarce moisture or high heat loads. Look for a claim that reverses the process or makes an unsupported generalisation.

right.text: local water source: a concentration of accessible water within a drier landscape.
right.explain: This distinction is correct: A local supply can support life without changing regional aridity. Look for a claim that reverses the process or makes an unsupported generalisation.

right.text: surface diversity: rocky stony and sandy surfaces rather than dunes alone.
right.explain: This distinction is correct: Desert classification concerns aridity, not one required surface material. Look for a claim that reverses the process or makes an unsupported generalisation.

wrong.text: One rain shower permanently ends climatic aridity.
wrong.explain: A brief event does not replace the longer-term moisture regime.

wrong.text: Every desert plant must have large permanently exposed soft leaves.
wrong.explain: Adaptations differ but commonly address scarce moisture or high heat loads.

wrong.text: One oasis proves that the surrounding desert is uniformly wet.
wrong.explain: A local supply can support life without changing regional aridity.

wrong.text: A place without dunes cannot be a desert.
wrong.explain: Desert classification concerns aridity, not one required surface material.
